Question_text: A student investigates the time taken for a light paper cup to fall to the floor. The student holds one paper cup, as shown in Fig. 1.1. The student drops the cup and measures the time t for it to fall to the floor.
image: Fig. 1.1 shows a diagram of a person's hand holding a single paper cup upright, about to drop it. The cup is depicted as a standard fluted paper cup, open at the top and closed at the bottom.

Parts.part_text: The student repeats the experiment and obtains the following five values for t, measured in seconds. 1.19 1.00 0.93 1.03 1.08
Calculate tav, the average value for t. Give your answer to two decimal places.
The student records his value for tav to more than two decimal places. Suggest why two decimal places is more suitable in this case.
The student finds it difficult to drop the cup and measure t. Suggest how two students working together can measure t more accurately.
The student repeats the experiment with two cups, as shown in Fig. 1.2.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.2 shows a diagram of two paper cups stacked one inside the other, indicating an increased mass for the falling object.

Parts.part_text: The experiment is repeated for an increasing number of cups. The results obtained are recorded in Fig. 1.3, where N is the number of cups. Add to Fig. 1.3 your value of tav for one cup from (a)(i). On Fig. 1.4, plot the graph of tav/s on the y-axis against N on the x-axis. Start your axes from tav = 0.5s and N = 0. Draw the smooth curve of best fit.
Parts.image: Fig. 1.3 displays a table with two columns, 'N' (number of cups) and 'tav/s' (average time in seconds), showing experimental data for falling cups: N=2, tav=0.89; N=3, tav=0.82; N=5, tav=0.69; N=7, tav=0.63; N=9, tav=0.61; N=11, tav=0.61. There's a blank row for N=1 to be filled by the student. Fig. 1.4 shows an empty graph grid with a y-axis starting from 0.5 and an x-axis starting from 0. The grid is ready for plotting tav/s against N, as instructed by the question.

Parts.part_text: When two quantities x and y are inversely proportional to each other, they obey the relationship x x y = constant. Use data from the graph or table to explain whether tav is inversely proportional to N.
It is important to drop the cup from the same height each time. Explain how the student does this without measuring the height.
Name the physical quantity being changed by increasing the number of cups.
The student accidentally stands on one cup. Explain why it should not be used in the investigation.
Suggest a reason why the last two values for tav in Fig. 1.3 are the same.

Question_text: A student investigates the behaviour of resistors.

Parts.part_text: Three resistors A, B and C are labelled 100Ω, 150Ω and 220Ω respectively.
Draw the arrangement of A, B and C that gives the largest possible total resistance.
Calculate the resistance of this arrangement.
Draw the arrangement of A, B and C that gives the smallest possible total resistance.
A fourth resistor is shown in Fig. 2.1. The resistor colour code is shown in Fig. 2.2. State the resistance of this resistor.
Parts.image: Fig. 2.1 shows a diagram of a resistor with three colour bands: brown, grey, brown, from left to right. Fig. 2.2 is a table showing the resistor colour code, mapping colours (black, brown, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, grey, white) to their corresponding numerical values (0-9).

Question_text: A laboratory thermometer is used to measure the temperature of oil in a test-tube. The thermometer is initially at room temperature.

Parts.part_text: State the temperature shown by the thermometer in Fig. 3.1.
Parts.image: Fig. 3.1 shows a mercury-in-glass thermometer. The scale ranges from -10 °C to 110 °C. The mercury level is visible and appears to be at 22 °C.

Parts.part_text: A test-tube of oil is heated in a bath of very hot water for 15 minutes, as shown in Fig. 3.2.
Parts.image: Fig. 3.2 shows an experimental setup for heating oil in a test-tube. A test-tube containing 'oil' is placed inside a beaker labeled 'water bath at 90°C'. The beaker is supported by a 'gauze' on a 'tripod', and heat is applied from below, labeled 'HEAT'. The water level in the beaker is clearly depicted as being higher than the oil level in the test-tube.

Parts.part_text: Explain why the level of oil in the test-tube should be below the level of water in the water bath.
A student removes the test-tube from the water bath. He then places the thermometer in the oil. Describe how the reading on the thermometer changes over the next few minutes.
Describe how the student reads the thermometer accurately.

A second student repeats the experiment in (b) using a temperature sensor instead of a thermometer. The temperature sensor is connected to a data logger. The data logger records the temperature every 0.1 s for 20 minutes. On the axes shown in Fig. 3.3, sketch the shape of the graph produced by the data logger.
Parts.image: Fig. 3.3 shows an empty graph grid with the y-axis labeled 'temperature / °C' and the x-axis labeled 'time / minutes', with an origin at (0,0) and an x-axis marker at 20 minutes. The graph is intended for sketching a cooling curve.

Question_text: Fig. 4.1 shows a triangular cardboard lamina with three small holes. Describe an experiment to find the position of the centre of mass of the lamina. You may use any common laboratory equipment. Your answer must include a labelled diagram of the apparatus being used.
image: Fig. 4.1 shows a triangular cardboard lamina with its vertices slightly rounded. There are three small circles marked near the edges of the triangle, representing small holes. The word 'lamina' points to the triangular shape.
